_doc: THE WORN PATHS AND TRAILS OF 1812 (T-3339). Drawn by renderers/web/js/yards.js as ribbons of trodden earth draped on the committed ground, the sward thinned under them. NOT ONE COORDINATE HERE IS AUTHORED: each line is the least-cost route over the 1812 ground between derived end points, smoothed and given a slow wander, written by tools/generate_worn_ground_1812.py (its docstring is the rule and the sources) and re-derived byte for byte by tools/check.sh. docs/LIBERTIES.md L-t3339-worn-ground-1812.
name: The worn paths and trails of 1812
coordinates: Local East-North-Up metres from data/datum.json's origin.

existence.note: Each trail states its own existence and sources; every alignment is reconstructed.

runs_note: EMPTY, AND DELIBERATELY: these are trodden lines on open ground, not fences.

ground.note: Each trail names its own treatment and form: `tread` a single worn foot-and-hoof line, `two_track` a cart's two ruts with a lighter median, `band` a broad trodden way. `wear` (0..1) is how bare it is, set by the traffic the sources and the buildings imply; the faintest are barely there.

trails.name: The fort's road south, from the main gate down the river to the outlet

existence.note: The evacuation column of 15 August 1812 - soldiers, a 'train of wagons' with the women and children, two officers' wives on horseback (Currey) - went this way out of the gate to the lake shore, and the beaten trail it took (Andreas) left from here. A garrison's carts, the Lee family's and the traders' traffic to the outlet would have worn it into a two-rut track.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the gate to the Lee house, keeping about 32 m back from the old channel's west bank

trails.name: The beaten Indian trail along the lake shore, south toward Fort Wayne and Detroit

existence.note: Andreas: 'Along the lake shore ran a beaten Indian trail, which was the path pursued', the sand hills about a hundred yards west of it. Quaife (1923): the road from Detroit 'followed the beach the remaining sixty miles to Chicago'. On sand the tread shows faintly.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the committed evacuation route (data/terrain/1812_evacuation_route.geojson) set 18 m inland of the waterline it follows, so the tread runs on the dry upper beach

trails.name: The Vincennes trace, the Potawatomi trail south to the Wabash

existence.note: Quaife (1923, ch. III): an ancient Potawatomi thoroughfare from Lake Michigan to the Wabash; Captain Heald rode up it with his bride in the spring of 1811, and in August 1812 the Wabash bands 'hastened northward with utmost speed along the ancient trail'. It became Hubbard's trail and, in 1834, the State road, which 'was forced to follow the old track'. Latrobe (1833, in Andreas) on such a trail near Chicago: 'the deep, black, narrow trail'.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: from the fork at the outlet, the least-cost route to the 1835 scene's reconstructed State road (data/streets/1835.json state_road_south, L381) and that line south to the box's edge, so the undeveloped land reads the same in 1812 and 1835

trails.name: The path along the river's south bank, from the agency to the forks

existence.note: Currey (1912): the man and boy escaping Lee's Place in April 1812 ran 'toward the fort' and 'reached the river somewhere near the present location of State Street bridge', calling across to Burns, then ran on along the bank to the fort. Whistler's draught and Quaife (1913) put the company cornfield and a house at the forks, which the garrison worked.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the interpreter's house to the Clark house, keeping about 28 m back from the south bank; it fords the State Street creek near its mouth

trails.name: The path up the South Branch's east bank, toward Lee's Place

existence.note: Currey (1912): from the haystacks on the east side of the river at Lee's Place the two 'made a run for the woods which were near at hand and directed their course toward the fort'. Andreas: the Hardscrabble cabin stood 'near the most frequented trail that led to the Desplaines'. Lightly worn: a farm three miles out.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the forks to the farm's haystacks, keeping about 45 m back from the east bank, through the bank timber

trails.name: Lee's Place: the path from the cabin down to the canoes

existence.note: Currey (1912): the discharged soldier 'walked in a deliberate manner down the path toward the canoes tied up at the river bank'.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: straight from the cabin's river front to the bank, down the bank's normal the cabin is seated on

trails.name: The path along the north bank, from the Kinzie house to the Burns house

existence.note: Currey (1912): Mrs. Kinzie, at the Burns house, 'ran to her own home, a quarter of a mile distant'. Ouilmette's, Lalime's and Lemai's houses stood along the same bank between them.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the Kinzie house to the Burns house, keeping about 22 m back from the north bank

trails.name: From the main gate round to the wharf

existence.note: Whistler's 1808 draught places the building; that a path was worn to it is this project's reading. The landing the drafter numbers 27, 122 ft from the pickets: boats, water and stores came and went by it.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the fort's road (or the gate) to the door

trails.name: To the stables

existence.note: Whistler's 1808 draught places the building; that a path was worn to it is this project's reading. Horses led out and in, and the hay and dung carried, every day.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the fort's road (or the gate) to the door

trails.name: To the agent's house and the factory

existence.note: Whistler's 1808 draught places the building; that a path was worn to it is this project's reading. The Indian agency and the United States factory, where the trade was done.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the fort's road (or the gate) to the door

trails.name: The Kinzie house down to its landing, across from the fort

existence.note: Wau-Bun, through Currey (1912): 'by means of two old pirogues, or dugouts, that were kept moored near the house', the family crossed to the fort. The house faced the river across its 'broad green space', so one path crossed the green.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: from the front door straight down to the bank opposite the fort

trails.name: A camp path between the far west and head west groups

existence.note: Currey (1912): 'groups of Indian wigwams clustered along the creek', the Potawatomi's 'favorite camping place'. That the groups wore paths between them is this project's reading of a camp of some seven hundred people a few dozen metres apart.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route between the two groups' worn edges, round every other group; a short link the spanning tree left out

trails.name: The upper group's path down to the water

existence.note: Wau-Bun ch. XIX: at the wigwam Mrs. Helm was led to, water was dipped 'from a stream that flowed near'. Every lodge carried its water, every day, so each group wore a path to the bank, and the groups behind ran theirs into it.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the group's worn edge to the dry bank above the nearest open water, ending where it meets a water path already worn

trails.name: The camp's path to the agency and the factory

existence.note: The gathering had come for the factory's goods and the agent's council (Wau-Bun ch. XVIII: the council 'on the afternoon of the 12th'; the goods given out on the 14th). The traffic between the camp and the agency would have worn the camp's busiest line.

trails.alignment: reconstructed: the least-cost route from the nearest group (mouth) toward the agent's house door, beside the factory, ending where it meets the south-bank path that runs on to it

assertions.claim: no vertex of any trail lies on water, except where the two bank paths and the camp paths marked `fords` cross a creek (the renderer leaves the ford's wet ground undrawn)
no vertex of any trail lies on a structure's footprint (grown 1.2 m) other than the picket row its gate opens in and the wharf it ends at
no trail's edge comes within 1.2 m of a tree a 1812 planting record stands
